passages.text: STARS, FIXED, those heavenly bodies which constantly keep the same situation with respect to one another, and are thus distinguished from the planets and comets.
They shine by their own native light, and not by light borrowed from the sun, as the planets do; and this light is thought to proceed from fire, like that of the sun.
It is most probable that every fixed star is a sun, as large and bright as our own, and that each is attended by planets which revolve about it.
Their distance is so great that no sensible parallax has yet been discovered in any of them, even with the finest instruments.
The milky way, which some of the ancients took for a vapour, is found by Dr Herschel's telescopes to consist of an innumerable multitude of small stars, too remote to be seen singly by the naked eye.
As the stars are probably of the same nature and magnitude, those which appear brightest are judged to be the nearest, and the faintest the most remote.

Yet Dr Halley observed that Sirius, Arcturus, and Aldebaran have changed their places since the time of Ptolemy; so that the stars are not strictly fixed, though their motion is too slow to be perceived in the life of man.
A star is a luminous spheroid of plasma held together by its own gravity. The nearest star to Earth is the Sun.
For most of its active life, a star shines because of nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core. The energy then travels out and leaves the surface as light and heat.
Many stars have planets. Planets around other stars were first confirmed in the 1990s, and thousands of such exoplanets are now known.
Friedrich Bessel made the first successful measurement of a stellar parallax in 1838, for the star 61 Cygni. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.
The Sun is one of billions of stars in the Milky Way galaxy. The band of light called the Milky Way is the combined light of stars too faint to see one by one.
Stars differ greatly in mass, size and luminosity. How bright a star looks from Earth depends on both its luminosity and its distance.
Stars are not fixed. Each has a proper motion across the sky, too small to notice over a human lifetime without instruments. Edmond Halley first detected the proper motion of stars in 1718.
Stars form from collapsing clouds of gas and dust. When a star uses up the fuel in its core, it changes and ends as a white dwarf, a neutron star or a black hole.

reasons: Same subject: STARS, FIXED and Star.
Rare terms appear in both: parallax, Milky Way, Halley, proper motion of stars.
Milky Way scores well but covers only one part of the entry.

alignments.label: Same place always

britannica.quote: constantly keep the same situation with respect to one another

alignments.note: To the eye this holds. The stars do move, but too slowly to see in a lifetime. The entry itself makes this point in B7.

alignments.label: Light from fire

britannica.quote: this light is thought to proceed from fire, like that of the sun

wikipedia.quote: a star shines because of nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core

alignments.note: Right that stars make their own light. The source is nuclear fusion, not burning. This is a change in knowledge.

alignments.label: Each star a sun

britannica.quote: every fixed star is a sun

wikipedia.quote: The nearest star to Earth is the Sun

alignments.note: The same idea in new words. Today the Sun is called a star, where 1797 called each star a sun.

alignments.label: Planets round stars

britannica.quote: each is attended by planets which revolve about it

wikipedia.quote: Planets around other stars were first confirmed in the 1990s

alignments.note: A guess in 1797 with no evidence. Observers confirmed it about two hundred years later. Not every star is known to have planets.

alignments.label: No parallax found

britannica.quote: no sensible parallax has yet been discovered

wikipedia.quote: Friedrich Bessel made the first successful measurement of a stellar parallax in 1838

alignments.note: True in 1797, and the word "yet" leaves room for later work. Bessel measured the first parallax 41 years later.

alignments.label: Milky Way is stars

britannica.quote: an innumerable multitude of small stars

wikipedia.quote: the combined light of stars too faint to see one by one

alignments.note: Herschel's view holds. Wikipedia adds that the Sun itself is one of the stars of the Milky Way galaxy.

alignments.label: Brightness shows distance

britannica.quote: those which appear brightest are judged to be the nearest

wikipedia.quote: Stars differ greatly in mass, size and luminosity

alignments.note: Stars are not all alike. A bright star can be far away and very luminous. This is a change in knowledge.

alignments.label: Halley's moving stars

britannica.quote: Sirius, Arcturus, and Aldebaran have changed their places since the time of Ptolemy

wikipedia.quote: Edmond Halley first detected the proper motion of stars in 1718

alignments.note: Both texts credit Halley. Wikipedia names the motion proper motion.

alignments.label: Stars are born and die

wikipedia.quote: Stars form from collapsing clouds of gas and dust

alignments.note: The 1797 entry treats the stars as lasting for ever. Wikipedia describes how stars form and how they end.

suggestedQuestions: Did the 1797 entry guess that other stars have planets?
Are the fixed stars really fixed?
Why could astronomers in 1797 not measure the distance to a star?

Did the 1797 entry guess that other star.answer: Yes. It called it most probable that every fixed star is a sun with planets that revolve about it [B3]. This was a guess. Wikipedia says planets around other stars were first confirmed in the 1990s, and thousands are now known [W3].

Are the fixed stars really fixed?.answer: No. The 1797 entry defines them by their fixed places [B1], but it also reports that Halley found Sirius, Arcturus and Aldebaran had moved since Ptolemy [B7]. Wikipedia says every star has a proper motion, first detected by Halley in 1718 [W7].

Why could astronomers in 1797 not measur.answer: The stars were too far away. The entry says no parallax had yet been found, even with the finest instruments [B4]. Wikipedia says Bessel made the first successful measurement in 1838, and the nearest star after the Sun is about 4.2 light-years away [W4].
